meta.date: ~124–121 BC (476 years after Lehi left Jerusalem)

world_behind.title: The covenant is registered
world_behind.text: Verse 1 has Benjamin taking the names of everyone who entered it. Nehemiah's covenant renewal produced a sealed document with names attached, and Ezra records people searched for in a register and not found. A covenant that can be joined is a covenant with a list, and this is the record's only one.

world_behind.title: Unanimous, with one stated exception
world_behind.text: Not one soul except little children. The exemption matches exactly what the angel said two chapters earlier, that children are blessed and blameless. The list was drawn up on a doctrine.

world_behind.title: The camp breaks up
world_behind.text: Every family returns to its own house, in the same household units that pitched the tents in Mosiah 2. The record closes the scene it opened, and the reader is left looking at an empty field.

world_behind.title: A working king, for the second generation
world_behind.text: Benjamin had labored with his own hands so the people would not be taxed; Mosiah tills the earth so as not to be burdensome. Paul used the same reasoning about his own trade (2 Thes. 3:8). The practice is now inherited.

words.text: Modern English keeps this word for the convenient thing done instead of the right one. Treated at 1 Nephi 10:15. The sense here is close to the reverse. It means fitting, or called for by the case, and Paul uses it that way when he says all things are lawful but all things are not expedient. Benjamin is not judging that a list would be handy. He is judging that the occasion requires one.

The word turns over between the chapter's first two verses. First it is plural and administrative, the names of the covenanters written down at the king's direction. Then it is singular and belongs to someone else, taken upon them rather than carried from birth. Two senses one verse apart, and the record sets them next to each other without remark.

Set apart formally, and the same verb the record used when Nephi consecrated Jacob and Joseph as priests. Treated at 2 Nephi 1:7. Benjamin consecrates his own son as king. Kingship and priesthood are being conferred by the same act, which is how the office has worked in this book since Mosiah 1:16.

A charge is a duty formally laid on a person, and the plural gathers several of them. Treated at 2 Nephi 20:6. Benjamin had handed over the affairs of the kingdom and then the records and relics in two separate acts back in Mosiah 1:15; here both are summed as "all the charges concerning the kingdom" (v. 3). The plural is used nowhere else in the record, though Chronicles uses it for the duties assigned to priests by course. The itemizing had already been done, so the handover needs only this phrase.

cites.quote: all the charges concerning the kingdom

spans.text: all the charges concerning the kingdom

words.text: The ordinal, used here of a man's age. The record uses the word nine times and the King James Bible nine. Verse 4 dates the accession by how old Mosiah was, the way the books of Kings date a reign. Every later use in this record counts years of the reign of the judges, so this is the last Nephite date that hangs on a person.

Heavy to carry, and the sense here is fiscal. Paul told two congregations he worked so as not to be chargeable to them. Mosiah tills the earth for the same stated reason, which makes an agricultural detail a statement about the cost of government.

phrases.term: He should take the names of all those who had entered into a covenant
phrases.text: Administration immediately after revelation. The angel's message, the falling down, the mighty change, and the new name are followed by a clerk's task. The record treats the list as the natural next step and spends one verse on it.

phrases.term: There was not one soul, except it were little children
phrases.text: Total participation, reported without celebration. The exception is stated in the same clause and left unexplained, because the angel explained it already. It is the only unanimous covenant in the record.

phrases.term: To stir them up in remembrance of the oath which they had made
phrases.text: The priests' assignment is memory. Benjamin had used the same phrase of the director in the wilderness (Mosiah 1:17), where affliction stirred people up in remembrance of duty. Here the stirring is a standing office with people appointed to it.

phrases.term: They returned, every one, according to their families, to their own houses
phrases.text: The same unit that camped is the unit that leaves. Tents pitched by household, doors toward the temple, and now households walking home. The sentence does the work of a closing stage direction.

phrases.term: About four hundred and seventy-six years from the time that Lehi left Jerusalem
phrases.text: The record dates itself from a departure rather than from a founding, a reign, or a creation. Every chronological notice in these books counts from the moment a family walked out of a city, a choice about what the beginning was.

phrases.term: Did walk in the ways of the Lord, and did observe his judgments and his statutes
phrases.text: Statutes are fixed enactments and judgments are decisions in cases; the pair is Deuteronomy's standard shorthand for the whole law, and applying it here measures Mosiah against Israel's kings rather than against his own predecessors. It is a verdict in the vocabulary of Kings, delivered before any evidence. The record grades Mosiah's whole reign and then gives a single supporting fact: that he farmed. It is a striking ratio of judgment to demonstration.

phrases.term: He also, himself, did till the earth
phrases.text: Two intensifiers on a small verb. The record insists that the king personally did the work, gives the fiscal reason in the next clause, and grounds it in his father's practice in the one after. Continuity between two reigns is established by manual labor.

verses.label: v. 3
verses.title: Four royal acts run together
verses.text: The verse runs the whole transfer of government together without a break: the son consecrated ruler and king, the charges concerning the kingdom given, priests appointed to teach, and the multitude dismissed. Each of the four could have carried its own verse, and the assembly that occupied Mosiah 2 through 5 is closed out by the last clause. The record spends four chapters on the speech and one sentence on the succession.

verses.label: v. 4
verses.title: A running total from Lehi's departure
verses.text: The record supplies an absolute date: "making in the whole, about four hundred and seventy-six years from the time that Lehi left Jerusalem." Seven such totals appear across the record, at 2 Nephi 5:28, Jacob 1:1, Enos 1:25, here, Mosiah 29:46, 3 Nephi 1:1, and 3 Nephi 2:6. The next one balances against this one: Mosiah 29:46 gives 509 years and a reign of thirty-three, and 476 plus 33 is 509. Two books apart, the arithmetic agrees to the year.

verses.label: v. 5
verses.title: A reign and a life closed in nine words
verses.text: The record gives Benjamin's death the shortest sentence in the chapter: "And king Benjamin lived three years and he died." No burial, no mourning, no summary of his character. The contrast is with the space just spent on him, since Mosiah 2 through 5 is his voice almost without interruption, and it stops here without ceremony.

verses.label: v. 7
verses.title: A peace measured in the same number as a life
verses.text: The chapter's last clause gives a span: "there was no contention among all his people for the space of three years." Verse 5 has given the same figure for Benjamin's remaining years. Whether the record intends the two threes to be the same three years is not stated, and the chapter simply ends there, with a number that could be read either as a period of overlap or as a period that follows.

chapter.title: Seven verses close six chapters
chapter.text: Everything the address set up is discharged here: the covenant recorded, the name taken, the successor installed, the priests appointed, the crowd dismissed. The record does not linger, and the brevity is the point. The work of the assembly was done in the assembly.

chapter.title: The covenant produces a list
chapter.text: Verse 1 turns a covenant into paperwork, "he should take the names of all those who had entered into a covenant with God." Verse 2 reports the tally as a negative with one exception, "there was not one soul, except it were little children, but who had entered into the covenant." The same administrative reflex produces the consecrated priests of verse 3, the church rolls implied by Alma 1:24 and Alma 6:3 where names are blotted out, and the counting language of Mosiah 25:2–3.

chapter.title: The one exemption rests on an earlier argument
chapter.text: The single exception to the covenant is stated flatly and never justified here, because the angel justified it two chapters back. The record trusts its own prior reasoning enough not to restate it.

chapter.title: The succession is completed without ceremony
chapter.text: Consecrated, charged, and reigning, all inside one verse, alongside the appointment of priests and the dismissal of a crowd. A throne changes hands with less narrative attention than the tent arrangements received in Mosiah 2.

chapter.title: A king is graded before he governs
chapter.text: Verse 6 delivers the verdict; verse 7 supplies one fact. The record is confident enough about what makes a good reign to state the conclusion first, and the evidence it chooses is that the king worked his own ground.

chapter.title: Peace is measured against a life
chapter.text: Benjamin lives three years; there is no contention for three years. The record puts the two numbers four verses apart and draws no connection, and the reader is left to notice that the peace and the old king ended together.

applications.title: Write the name down
applications.text: After a decision that matters, record it somewhere with your name on it. Benjamin's next act after the covenant was to make it a document.

applications.title: Appoint someone to remind you
applications.text: The priests' job was to stir the people up in remembrance of what they had promised. Ask someone to hold you to a specific commitment, and tell them exactly what it is.

applications.title: Send everyone home in good order
applications.text: The assembly ended deliberately, by families. When something intense finishes, give it a proper close.

applications.title: Do the work yourself
applications.text: Mosiah farmed so as not to be a burden. Find the place where your position lets you offload something, and do that thing yourself for a season.

applications.title: Continue what was handed to you
applications.text: Verse 7 has Mosiah keeping up his father's practice in everything. Name one thing you inherited that is worth keeping, and keep it on purpose.

applications.title: Notice when the peace is borrowed
applications.text: Three years of quiet that coincide with an old man's last three years. Ask what stability in your life is resting on someone who will not always be there.

questions.text: What have I committed to that exists nowhere in writing?
Am I in or out of the things I claim to belong to, and would a list show it?
Who stirs me up in remembrance, and have I actually given them permission?
If my life were summarized in one sentence of that kind, what would it say?
Where am I letting my position spare me work that I could do?
What am I doing because my parents did it, and do I know why?
